02 · INDUSTRY MOMENTUM

Why is quant finance so popular today?

25%

Quant / systematic strategies now represent a large share of hedge fund assets

The chart highlights the expansion of quant hedge fund AUM over time, showing that systematic strategies have become a major part of the industry.

+3.46%

Recent style-level return leadership

In the comparison shown, systematic equity L/S strategies outperformed fundamental peers in September 2026.

Main reasons quant finance is becoming more popular

✓Data-rich markets: more market, alternative, and digital data than ever before.
✓Computing power: cheaper cloud computing, faster optimization, and scalable simulation.
✓Automation: institutions want systematic, repeatable, and monitorable decision processes.
✓Cross-disciplinary talent: finance now attracts mathematicians, programmers, physicists, and AI specialists.
Interpret carefully: this slide illustrates industry momentum, not a universal claim that quant always outperforms. Performance varies by market regime, costs, model quality, and risk management.

Every trade faces liquidity and market-impact constraints.

Why market microstructure matters

›Price discovery: orders continuously update quoted prices.
›Execution quality: signals must survive spreads and fees.
›Latency and depth: speed is useful only with sound controls.
In digital markets, a forecast becomes profit only after a trade can be executed.

Four risks to manage

Model / data drift

Markets change; calibration and signal strength decay.

Correlated AI behavior

Shared models or signals may intensify crowding.

Provider concentration

Dependence on the same cloud and model infrastructure.

Cyber / manipulation

Data poisoning, prompt injection, fraud and outages.

A controlled deployment process

01Document data lineage, intended use and model ownership.
02Validate independently against benchmarks and stress tests.

04Reassess models when markets, vendors or data change.
Trustworthy AI in finance requires lifecycle governance—not only an accuracy metric.

b c > a d

THEOREM 4 · BELLMAN RECURSION AND BASELINE CERTIFICATE

Risk-aware sampled control has a conditional guarantee

OPTIMIZE: HIT PROBABILITY + NONNEGATIVE PREMIUM BURDEN
Vn(z) = minr ∈ A(z) { Hnr(z) + Cnr(z) + Qnr Vn+1(z) }
H = immediate hit risk

Probability of crossing a failure threshold before the next decision.

C = policy burden

Nonnegative cost of charging an additional premium.

Q = safe continuation

Probability-weighted future risk on surviving paths.

BASELINE IS A FEASIBLE CANDIDATE
Optimal risk + burden ≤ Base failure risk

The Bellman claim is for the specified transition law, candidate actions and decision schedule.

NON-DETERIORATION CERTIFICATE
Dn ≥ 0 on every live state

A nonnegative baseline-risk residual yields a weak guarantee; strict improvement needs positive visited residual.

Tune the feedback, do not maximize it

Calibrate before real deployment

Verify market and transaction responses, model law errors and numerical approximation.

eβ

One unit of log TVL

OTHER LONGITUDINAL ESTIMATES · AVOID SAFETY CLAIMS

Protocol age and prior hacks complicate the story

NEWER PROTOCOLS
0.133
Hazard ratio for log protocol age
p < 0.001. Conditional on scale and calendar quarter, more recently established protocols appear more frequently in new listings.
PRIOR PUBLIC HACK
1.571
Hazard ratio with wide uncertainty
95% CI: 0.172–14.365; p = 0.689. No precise directional evidence.
INTERPRETATION
Selection ≠ Safety
Newer protocols can attract protection demand; observed hacks can either deter capital or increase attention.
Risk group, cohort dynamics, and unobserved decisions still matter.
Do not interpret a lower age hazard ratio as proof that older code is less safe—or the hack estimate as evidence hacks help insurability.

CAUSALITY, MEASUREMENT, AND MARKET BOUNDARIES

What the evidence can—and cannot—establish

STRONGER CLAIMS SUPPORTED
On-chain event timestamps support a documented history of observed first listings.
Lagged TVL is associated with listing among active protocols.
Current capacity, availability, and quoted prices show different patterns.
Reviewed exact product–protocol links reduce ambiguous classification.
CLAIMS NOT SUPPORTED
Insurance listing proves smart-contract safety or will guarantee a claim payment.
Cover causes TVL growth or leads to lower future hack probability.
A quoted annual price is a pure actuarial expected loss estimate.
Single-provider public data capture the complete insurance market.
Key limitations: 25 primary listing events, left-censored history, possible missing failed protocols, public-data revisions, and unobserved purchases, claims and shared-pool constraints.

How practitioners should use an insurability signal

FOUR QUESTIONS FOR DEFI USERS, TREASURIES, AND RISK TEAMS
01 · IdentifyIs the named insured object the exact protocol, version, or another product?
→
02 · EvaluateWhat are the technical, liquidity, oracle, governance and dependency risks?
→
03 · Read the termsWhat are current available capacity, exclusions, price, and claims conditions?
→
04 · MonitorTrack stress, policy changes, product status and actual protection over time.
USEFUL AS
A screening signal for market relevance, assessability and underwriting attention
NOT VALID AS
A consumer safety score, investment recommendation or guarantee of successful claims
This workflow is a practical interpretation of the study, not an experimentally tested intervention.

CONCLUSION · OPEN QUESTIONS · FUTURE RESEARCH

Digital underwriting is more transparent—not risk-free

THE EMPIRICAL MESSAGE
Public cover reveals market selection and capital allocation.
It does not certify protocol safety.
01 · ADOPTIONSelection is conditional

Scale matters primarily among economically active protocols.

02 · CAPITALDepth and quotes differ

Larger covered protocols generally show more available capacity and lower prices.

03 · VALIDITYDo not equate cover with quality

Market attention, demand and risk-based selection can coexist.

Next frontier: multi-provider histories of purchases, capacity, quoted terms, claims, governance decisions and cross-protocol dependencies.
